evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a JAMA Network Open cohort study (plus its online supplement) that used a large US insurance claims and electronic health record database (Optum Market Clarity, 2016-2022) to estimate the health care costs of Lyme disease (LD) for 70,531 identified case patients, comparing localized, disseminated, and indeterminate disease. The study explicitly excludes indirect costs (lost wages, caregiver time) and does not capture costs beyond a 6-month follow-up window, so it does not speak to longer-term persistent-symptom burden.

contextual_issues: Indirect costs (lost income/wages, productivity loss, caregiver time) are explicitly stated as not included in the cost estimates or extrapolation ('This estimation does not include all states or indirect costs').

The 6-month follow-up window is stated by the authors as potentially 'too short to capture the costs for patients with persistent symptoms,' implying a possible undercount of costs for patients with longer-term or relapsing symptoms, but this is not quantified.

Diagnostic delay and repeated pre-diagnosis care-seeking are only partly addressed: the 30-day pre-index period was included in the follow-up window specifically 'to capture costs possibly incurred during diagnostic workup before an LD diagnosis,' but no separate diagnostic-delay cost or time estimate is reported.

Previously observed racial/ethnic differences in LD surveillance case counts and disease severity at diagnosis are cited (Gould et al. 2024, 2025) as the rationale for collecting race/ethnicity data, but this study itself does not report a quantified cost or outcome disparity by race or ethnicity.

The study population is restricted to insured individuals in Optum Market Clarity with continuous enrollment; the authors state this 'may not be generalizable to all patients with LD,' implying uninsured or discontinuously insured patients' costs and access barriers are not captured.
evidence_gaps: Would need a linked labor-force, disability, or caregiver-time survey to estimate indirect costs (lost wages, productivity loss, caregiving time) associated with LD, which this claims-based study does not capture.

Would need extended longitudinal follow-up beyond 6 months, or a validated case definition for post-treatment/persistent LD symptoms, to estimate costs for patients whose symptoms persist past the study's follow-up window.

Would need validation of the localized/disseminated/indeterminate classification algorithm (stated by the authors as not independently validated) and of the underlying CDC case-identification algorithm outside high-incidence states before extrapolating costs nationally.
Would need an uninsured/underinsured population cost data source, since Optum Market Clarity captures only insured patients with continuous enrollment.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the 4 cost-estimation methods (episode analysis, cases-as-self-controls, unadjusted case-control, multivariable-adjusted case-control) into one point estimate or simple low-to-high range: they use different populations (e.g., N=70,531 for episode analysis vs N=64,893 self-controls vs N=64,891 matched cases/168,509 controls) and structurally different measurement time windows (a variable-length LD episode that the authors allowed to extend beyond 12 months, vs a fixed 6-month baseline/follow-up window), so differences in point estimates reflect methodology, not only confidence.

Do not add patient out-of-pocket (OOP) cost figures on top of the direct (standardized) cost figures: the authors explicitly state they 'did not compare OOP costs to the estimated direct costs because OOP costs were not standardized,' and OOP costs are a subset of total allowed health plan payments, not an additional cost layer.

Do not pool the extrapolated national/high-incidence-state cost burden figures ($591M-$1.05B, 2022 USD) with the per-patient or per-episode cost figures: the extrapolation applies only to a modeled 295,339 annual LD cases in 16 high-incidence states/DC (derived by multiplying an external estimate of 476,000 total US annual diagnosed/treated LD cases from Kugeler et al. 2021 by 81% located in high-incidence states and by a 0.766 positive predictive value from Kluberg et al. 2025), not to the 70,531-person study cohort or to the full US.

Do not conflate the national pooled 6-month cost-difference estimates (Tables 3-5) with the neighboring/non-neighboring state-stratified subgroup estimates in the supplement (eTables 6-11): for the indeterminate LD subgroup specifically, the self-controls cost difference reached significance in the national pooled analysis (p<.001) but did NOT reach statistical significance in either the neighboring-states stratum (p=0.576) or the non-neighboring-states stratum (p=0.128) for direct costs, nor in OOP costs (p=0.484 neighboring; p=0.903 non-neighboring).

Do not directly compare this study's 2022-CPI-standardized cost figures with the unadjusted historical cost figures from Zhang et al. (2000) or Hook et al. (2014-2016) cited in the Discussion without applying the same inflation adjustments and accounting for differing cost-estimation methods (e.g., practitioner charges vs patient-reported utilization vs standardized insurer-allowed amounts) that the authors themselves note make comparison difficult.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The indeterminate LD classification subgroup had a notably higher proportion of female patients (57.7%) compared with the localized (50.4%) and disseminated (50.5%) subgroups; sex distribution was otherwise roughly balanced overall (51.3% female, 48.7% male among all 70,531 case patients). No cost or outcome difference by sex is reported in this study.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: LD case patients were identified from Optum Market Clarity medical/pharmacy claims and EHR data using ICD-10 diagnosis codes (A69.xx) combined with antibiotic treatment claims, per a CDC claims-based case-identification algorithm; cost figures (direct and OOP) are all derived from this claims/EHR-coded cohort, and the localized/disseminated/indeterimate classification algorithm itself is explicitly noted by the authors as 'not validated.'

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The headline cost figures (e.g., $2227 episode cost, $3304 self-controls difference, $4098 case-control difference, $5571 adjusted case-control difference, and the $591M-$1.05B extrapolated national burden) are reported pooled by LD classification (localized/disseminated/indeterminate) and by state incidence status only; age, sex, race/ethnicity, and insurance type are used only as adjustment covariates in the multivariable model and are not reported as cost breakdowns by subgroup, and disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, and marital/familial status are not collected or reported at all.

decision_relevance.summary: This study provides claims-based, per-episode and 6-month per-patient direct and out-of-pocket cost figures for Lyme disease, stratified by disease severity (localized/disseminated/indeterminate) and by state LD-incidence status, plus a high-incidence-state national cost extrapolation. Patients and advocates could use the per-episode and OOP figures to understand typical insured-patient cost exposure for localized versus disseminated LD, while care delivery teams could use the cost-ratio and cost-difference figures to anticipate the resource burden of disseminated disease relative to localized disease. Payers and policymakers could use the high-incidence-state extrapolation ($591M-$1.05B, 2022 USD) as one input into estimating the aggregate economic burden of LD, provided they preserve the stated population, time-window, and methodological boundaries rather than treating it as a single precise national total or as inclusive of indirect costs.
use_cases: A patient or advocate audience could compare expected 6-month OOP cost ranges ($107-$401 per episode depending on disease classification) against their own insurance cost-sharing structure to anticipate out-of-pocket exposure for localized versus disseminated LD, while recognizing these figures reflect only the 15.5% insured subset with OOP data available.

A payer or policy audience could use the episode, self-controls, and case-control cost-difference estimates as separate (not averaged) inputs for high-incidence-state LD cost-burden modeling, explicitly excluding indirect costs and costs beyond 6 months, consistent with the study's own stated limitations.

contextual_issues: Indirect costs (lost income/wages, productivity loss, caregiver time) are explicitly stated as not included in the cost estimates or extrapolation ('This estimation does not include all states or indirect costs').

The 6-month follow-up window is stated by the authors as potentially 'too short to capture the costs for patients with persistent symptoms,' implying a possible undercount of costs for patients with longer-term or relapsing symptoms, but this is not quantified.

Diagnostic delay and repeated pre-diagnosis care-seeking are only partly addressed: the 30-day pre-index period was included in the follow-up window specifically 'to capture costs possibly incurred during diagnostic workup before an LD diagnosis,' but no separate diagnostic-delay cost or time estimate is reported.

Previously observed racial/ethnic differences in LD surveillance case counts and disease severity at diagnosis are cited (Gould et al. 2024, 2025) as the rationale for collecting race/ethnicity data, but this study itself does not report a quantified cost or outcome disparity by race or ethnicity.

The study population is restricted to insured individuals in Optum Market Clarity with continuous enrollment; the authors state this 'may not be generalizable to all patients with LD,' implying uninsured or discontinuously insured patients' costs and access barriers are not captured.
evidence_gaps: Would need a linked labor-force, disability, or caregiver-time survey to estimate indirect costs (lost wages, productivity loss, caregiving time) associated with LD, which this claims-based study does not capture.

Would need extended longitudinal follow-up beyond 6 months, or a validated case definition for post-treatment/persistent LD symptoms, to estimate costs for patients whose symptoms persist past the study's follow-up window.

Would need validation of the localized/disseminated/indeterminate classification algorithm (stated by the authors as not independently validated) and of the underlying CDC case-identification algorithm outside high-incidence states before extrapolating costs nationally.
Would need an uninsured/underinsured population cost data source, since Optum Market Clarity captures only insured patients with continuous enrollment.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the 4 cost-estimation methods (episode analysis, cases-as-self-controls, unadjusted case-control, multivariable-adjusted case-control) into one point estimate or simple low-to-high range: they use different populations (e.g., N=70,531 for episode analysis vs N=64,893 self-controls vs N=64,891 matched cases/168,509 controls) and structurally different measurement time windows (a variable-length LD episode that the authors allowed to extend beyond 12 months, vs a fixed 6-month baseline/follow-up window), so differences in point estimates reflect methodology, not only confidence.

Do not add patient out-of-pocket (OOP) cost figures on top of the direct (standardized) cost figures: the authors explicitly state they 'did not compare OOP costs to the estimated direct costs because OOP costs were not standardized,' and OOP costs are a subset of total allowed health plan payments, not an additional cost layer.

Do not pool the extrapolated national/high-incidence-state cost burden figures ($591M-$1.05B, 2022 USD) with the per-patient or per-episode cost figures: the extrapolation applies only to a modeled 295,339 annual LD cases in 16 high-incidence states/DC (derived by multiplying an external estimate of 476,000 total US annual diagnosed/treated LD cases from Kugeler et al. 2021 by 81% located in high-incidence states and by a 0.766 positive predictive value from Kluberg et al. 2025), not to the 70,531-person study cohort or to the full US.

Do not conflate the national pooled 6-month cost-difference estimates (Tables 3-5) with the neighboring/non-neighboring state-stratified subgroup estimates in the supplement (eTables 6-11): for the indeterminate LD subgroup specifically, the self-controls cost difference reached significance in the national pooled analysis (p<.001) but did NOT reach statistical significance in either the neighboring-states stratum (p=0.576) or the non-neighboring-states stratum (p=0.128) for direct costs, nor in OOP costs (p=0.484 neighboring; p=0.903 non-neighboring).

Do not directly compare this study's 2022-CPI-standardized cost figures with the unadjusted historical cost figures from Zhang et al. (2000) or Hook et al. (2014-2016) cited in the Discussion without applying the same inflation adjustments and accounting for differing cost-estimation methods (e.g., practitioner charges vs patient-reported utilization vs standardized insurer-allowed amounts) that the authors themselves note make comparison difficult.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The indeterminate LD classification subgroup had a notably higher proportion of female patients (57.7%) compared with the localized (50.4%) and disseminated (50.5%) subgroups; sex distribution was otherwise roughly balanced overall (51.3% female, 48.7% male among all 70,531 case patients). No cost or outcome difference by sex is reported in this study.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: LD case patients were identified from Optum Market Clarity medical/pharmacy claims and EHR data using ICD-10 diagnosis codes (A69.xx) combined with antibiotic treatment claims, per a CDC claims-based case-identification algorithm; cost figures (direct and OOP) are all derived from this claims/EHR-coded cohort, and the localized/disseminated/indeterimate classification algorithm itself is explicitly noted by the authors as 'not validated.'

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The headline cost figures (e.g., $2227 episode cost, $3304 self-controls difference, $4098 case-control difference, $5571 adjusted case-control difference, and the $591M-$1.05B extrapolated national burden) are reported pooled by LD classification (localized/disseminated/indeterminate) and by state incidence status only; age, sex, race/ethnicity, and insurance type are used only as adjustment covariates in the multivariable model and are not reported as cost breakdowns by subgroup, and disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, and marital/familial status are not collected or reported at all.

decision_relevance.summary: This study provides claims-based, per-episode and 6-month per-patient direct and out-of-pocket cost figures for Lyme disease, stratified by disease severity (localized/disseminated/indeterminate) and by state LD-incidence status, plus a high-incidence-state national cost extrapolation. Patients and advocates could use the per-episode and OOP figures to understand typical insured-patient cost exposure for localized versus disseminated LD, while care delivery teams could use the cost-ratio and cost-difference figures to anticipate the resource burden of disseminated disease relative to localized disease. Payers and policymakers could use the high-incidence-state extrapolation ($591M-$1.05B, 2022 USD) as one input into estimating the aggregate economic burden of LD, provided they preserve the stated population, time-window, and methodological boundaries rather than treating it as a single precise national total or as inclusive of indirect costs.
use_cases: A patient or advocate audience could compare expected 6-month OOP cost ranges ($107-$401 per episode depending on disease classification) against their own insurance cost-sharing structure to anticipate out-of-pocket exposure for localized versus disseminated LD, while recognizing these figures reflect only the 15.5% insured subset with OOP data available.

A payer or policy audience could use the episode, self-controls, and case-control cost-difference estimates as separate (not averaged) inputs for high-incidence-state LD cost-burden modeling, explicitly excluding indirect costs and costs beyond 6 months, consistent with the study's own stated limitations.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Direct Health Care Costs by Disease Severity (Optum Claims, 2016-2022)
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects claims/EHR-based direct (insurer-allowed) and out-of-pocket medical costs for insured Lyme disease patients in the Optum Market Clarity database, 2016-2022, stratified by localized vs disseminated disease, plus the study's own high-incidence-state annual cost extrapolation. It excludes indirect costs (lost wages, caregiver time), costs beyond a 6-month follow-up window, uninsured or discontinuously insured patients, and does not pool the study's four distinct cost-estimation methods or add out-of-pocket costs on top of direct costs.

takeaway.patient: This claims-based study found that patients with disseminated Lyme disease had a noticeably higher average direct medical cost per treatment episode than patients with localized disease, and a similar pattern held for the smaller group of patients whose out-of-pocket costs could be tracked. These figures only cover the first six months and do not include lost income, caregiving time, or costs for longer-lasting symptoms, so they likely understate total burden for anyone whose illness continues past that window.
takeaway.care: Disseminated Lyme disease cost roughly ten times more in out-of-pocket spending and several times more in direct episode costs than localized disease in this cohort, and disseminated cases (about 22% of all cases) accounted for nearly 69% of total episode costs - a concentration of resource use worth noting for care planning. The 'indeterminate' severity classification is not an independently validated algorithm, and its cost difference lost statistical significance when examined separately in neighboring-state and non-neighboring-state subgroups, suggesting this category's cost signal is less stable than the localized/disseminated comparison.
takeaway.policy: The study projects an annual direct health care cost burden for Lyme disease in 16 high-incidence states plus Washington, DC of roughly $591 million (episode-based lower bound) to $1.05 billion (case-control-based upper bound), in 2022 dollars, built on a projected 295,339 annual cases - these two bounds come from different methods with different populations and should be treated as separate scenarios, not averaged. This extrapolation excludes indirect costs and costs beyond six months, and the underlying per-patient cost figures are pooled across age, sex, race/ethnicity, and insurance type despite those being collected as covariates.

patient: If diagnosed with disseminated Lyme disease, ask your clinician what this might mean for your likely costs compared with earlier localized-stage disease, using this study's cost difference as a rough reference point rather than a guarantee for your own situation.

Keep in mind these figures only reflect the first six months after diagnosis and do not include lost income or caregiving costs, so if your symptoms continue longer, treat this as a partial picture of your financial burden.

Because only a small subset of patients in this study had trackable out-of-pocket cost data, compare these out-of-pocket figures to your own insurance plan's cost-sharing rules rather than assuming they apply directly to you.
care: Consider whether current care pathways and resource planning differentiate follow-up intensity between localized and disseminated Lyme disease, given the scale of cost difference reported here.

The non-significant cost differences for the 'indeterminate' classification in state-level subgroups may be worth checking against your own documentation and classification practices, since the authors themselves note this severity algorithm has not been independently validated.

Because the study's 6-month follow-up window may not capture costs for patients with persistent symptoms, a longer-term tracking or follow-up pathway for suspected persistent Lyme disease symptoms may be worth discussing with your team.
policy: Use the episode-based lower bound and case-control-based upper bound as separate scenario inputs for high-incidence-state cost burden modeling, rather than averaging them, consistent with the study's own methodological distinctions.

When using this extrapolation for budgeting or funding discussions, note explicitly that it excludes indirect costs (lost wages, caregiver time) and costs beyond six months, so total societal burden is likely understated.

Consider commissioning or supporting disaggregated cost analysis by age, sex, and race/ethnicity using federal survey sources (e.g., MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS), since this study's figures are pooled and not broken out by these subgroups despite collecting them as covariates.

## Parameters and Sources

All per-episode and out-of-pocket cost figures come from Table 2 (p.6) of a JAMA Network Open retrospective cohort study using the Optum Market Clarity claims/EHR database (2016-2022, 70,531 identified Lyme disease case patients), reported in 2022 CPI-adjusted dollars. The high-incidence-state extrapolation bounds come from eTable 12 (Supplement 1, p.2) and the Abstract/Conclusion, projecting 295,339 annual cases across 16 high-incidence states plus Washington, DC.

**Limitation - claims-based undercount:** Case patients were identified via ICD-10 codes (A69.xx) plus antibiotic treatment claims, and the localized/disseminated/indeterminate classification algorithm is explicitly described by the authors as not independently validated. These claims/EHR-derived figures likely undercount or misclassify some true Lyme disease burden.

**Limitation - subgroup disaggregation:** The headline cost figures (episode costs, cost differences, and the extrapolated national burden) are pooled by disease severity and state-incidence status only. Age, sex, race/ethnicity, and insurance type were used only as adjustment covariates, not reported as cost breakdowns by subgroup. Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this study did not perform it.

**Sex-based finding (not a cost finding):** The indeterminate classification subgroup had a notably higher share of female patients (57.7%) than the localized (50.4%) or disseminated (50.5%) subgroups; the study reports no cost or outcome difference by sex.

**Scope exclusions:** The authors explicitly exclude indirect costs (lost wages, caregiver time) and state the 6-month follow-up window may be "too short to capture the costs for patients with persistent symptoms," an unquantified likely undercount for longer-term illness. The study population is restricted to continuously insured patients, which the authors say "may not be generalizable to all patients with LD."

**Methodological note:** The document's four cost-estimation methods (episode analysis, self-controls, unadjusted case-control, adjusted case-control) use different populations and time windows and should not be pooled into one point estimate; the extrapolated $591M-$1.05B range reflects this methodological spread, not a confidence interval.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- LD-specific direct medical cost per episode, overall case patients: 2,227.00 in 2022 dollars is about 2,449.87 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Self-controls all-cause direct cost difference (6-month baseline vs follow-up), overall: 3,304.00 in 2022 dollars is about 3,634.65 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Unadjusted case-control all-cause direct cost difference, overall: 4,098.00 in 2022 dollars is about 4,508.12 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Multivariable-adjusted projected case-control direct cost difference, overall: 5,571.00 in 2022 dollars is about 6,128.53 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.100). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Direct Health Care Costs by Disease Severity (Optum Claims, 2016-2022)
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects claims/EHR-based direct (insurer-allowed) and out-of-pocket medical costs for insured Lyme disease patients in the Optum Market Clarity database, 2016-2022, stratified by localized vs disseminated disease, plus the study's own high-incidence-state annual cost extrapolation. It excludes indirect costs (lost wages, caregiver time), costs beyond a 6-month follow-up window, uninsured or discontinuously insured patients, and does not pool the study's four distinct cost-estimation methods or add out-of-pocket costs on top of direct costs.

takeaway.patient: This claims-based study found that patients with disseminated Lyme disease had a noticeably higher average direct medical cost per treatment episode than patients with localized disease, and a similar pattern held for the smaller group of patients whose out-of-pocket costs could be tracked. These figures only cover the first six months and do not include lost income, caregiving time, or costs for longer-lasting symptoms, so they likely understate total burden for anyone whose illness continues past that window.
takeaway.care: Disseminated Lyme disease cost roughly ten times more in out-of-pocket spending and several times more in direct episode costs than localized disease in this cohort, and disseminated cases (about 22% of all cases) accounted for nearly 69% of total episode costs - a concentration of resource use worth noting for care planning. The 'indeterminate' severity classification is not an independently validated algorithm, and its cost difference lost statistical significance when examined separately in neighboring-state and non-neighboring-state subgroups, suggesting this category's cost signal is less stable than the localized/disseminated comparison.
takeaway.policy: The study projects an annual direct health care cost burden for Lyme disease in 16 high-incidence states plus Washington, DC of roughly $591 million (episode-based lower bound) to $1.05 billion (case-control-based upper bound), in 2022 dollars, built on a projected 295,339 annual cases - these two bounds come from different methods with different populations and should be treated as separate scenarios, not averaged. This extrapolation excludes indirect costs and costs beyond six months, and the underlying per-patient cost figures are pooled across age, sex, race/ethnicity, and insurance type despite those being collected as covariates.

patient: If diagnosed with disseminated Lyme disease, ask your clinician what this might mean for your likely costs compared with earlier localized-stage disease, using this study's cost difference as a rough reference point rather than a guarantee for your own situation.

Keep in mind these figures only reflect the first six months after diagnosis and do not include lost income or caregiving costs, so if your symptoms continue longer, treat this as a partial picture of your financial burden.

Because only a small subset of patients in this study had trackable out-of-pocket cost data, compare these out-of-pocket figures to your own insurance plan's cost-sharing rules rather than assuming they apply directly to you.
care: Consider whether current care pathways and resource planning differentiate follow-up intensity between localized and disseminated Lyme disease, given the scale of cost difference reported here.

The non-significant cost differences for the 'indeterminate' classification in state-level subgroups may be worth checking against your own documentation and classification practices, since the authors themselves note this severity algorithm has not been independently validated.

Because the study's 6-month follow-up window may not capture costs for patients with persistent symptoms, a longer-term tracking or follow-up pathway for suspected persistent Lyme disease symptoms may be worth discussing with your team.
policy: Use the episode-based lower bound and case-control-based upper bound as separate scenario inputs for high-incidence-state cost burden modeling, rather than averaging them, consistent with the study's own methodological distinctions.

When using this extrapolation for budgeting or funding discussions, note explicitly that it excludes indirect costs (lost wages, caregiver time) and costs beyond six months, so total societal burden is likely understated.

Consider commissioning or supporting disaggregated cost analysis by age, sex, and race/ethnicity using federal survey sources (e.g., MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS), since this study's figures are pooled and not broken out by these subgroups despite collecting them as covariates.
